snippets: With October at 1.5% YoY, Q4 starts 0.3 percentage points above the SNB’s Q4 2026 conditional forecast of 1.2%: to meet it, November and December would need to average about 1.05%, which looks unlikely given that prices fell 0.2% MoM in November 2025. Inflation nonetheless remains within the 0–2% price-stability range. The next monetary policy assessment is on December 10th, after the November CPI and its rental update. At the September 24th press conference, Chairman Schlegel stressed that the SNB provides no forward guidance and will decide in December on the basis of the data, describing current monetary policy as supportive.

A closer look at the disaggregated data (Tables 1 and 2) confirms that, as in other advanced economies, housing rentals remain an important driver of inflation (see Chart 3). In Switzerland, this CPI component is updated every three months, in February, May, August, and November. October 2026 therefore delivers no new update: housing rentals were unchanged on the month and contributed nothing to the monthly change, and rental inflation remains at 1.6% YoY, the rate set by the August update, up from the 1.4% YoY that had held from the February (Q1) update through July.

In the medium term, the September forecast was slightly higher than in June, reflecting, among other things, the weakening of the Swiss franc, and remained within the range of price stability over the entire horizon, with annual average inflation projected at 0.7% YoY for 2026, 0.8% YoY for 2027, and 0.8% YoY for 2028, conditional on the SNB policy rate remaining at 0.0% throughout. On the exchange rate, the picture has shifted since March. Little is left of the appreciation pressure that followed the escalation of the conflict in the Middle East, when the franc was sought as a safe-haven currency, and the SNB raised its willingness to intervene.
In October 2026, the Swiss Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose by 1.5% year-on-year (YoY), up from the 1.0% YoY recorded in September and above the market consensus of 1.3% YoY.
